chunks.section: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
chunks.text: Athanasios Glentis † † thanks: Equal contribution, alphabetical order. Dawei Li 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Mingyi Hong Affiliation: University of Minnesota Email: {glent007,li004678,mhong}@umn.edu

Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the accumulated effective learning rate , C T = ∑ t < T η t / ∥ W t ∥ F C_{T}=\sum_{t<T}\eta_{t}/\lVert W_{t}\rVert_{F} , where η t \eta_{t} is the nominal learning rate and η t / ∥ W t ∥ F \eta_{t}/\lVert W_{t}\rVert_{F} is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs, with more relaxed weight-norm control.

Building on this connection between norm growth and exploration, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram–Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to t \sqrt{t} after t t steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Omega(\sqrt{T}) , with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about 15 % 15\% at matched validation loss to MuonH.

Optimizer design plays an important role in large language model (LLM) pretraining, shaping learning dynamics and model quality ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2026 ) . Understanding the principles behind successful optimizers is therefore essential for improving training. Weight-norm control is a common component of effective optimizers for LLM pretraining. AdamW and the weight-decay variant of Muon, MuonW, counter norm growth through decoupled shrinkage ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its strength must be tuned, and the resulting weight scale depends on the optimization dynamics. Explicit constraints provide more direct control, as in fixed-radius optimization ( Kodryan et al., 2022 ) , unit-norm weight vectors in nGPT ( Loshchilov et al., 2024 ) , and fixed weight and update norms in MuonH, the Hyperball variant of Muon ( Wen et al., 2026 ) . These constraints prescribe weight scales throughout training and leave less freedom for their evolution. These different norm controls raise a common question: When is norm control needed, why does it help, and how much is sufficient? Existing analyses explain important effects of weight norms on optimization ( Zhang et al., 2018 ; D’Angelo et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , but a unified basis for choosing among these controls remains incomplete. In particular, are the restrictions imposed by existing norm-control methods essential, or can weaker control deliver better optimization performance?

A common rationale for controlling weight norms is to prevent updates from becoming too small relative to the current weights. Following prior work ( D’Angelo et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , the effective learning rate is the ratio η t / ∥ W t ∥ F \eta_{t}/\lVert W_{t}\rVert_{F} of the nominal learning rate η t \eta_{t} to the Frobenius norm of the current weight matrix W t W_{t} . It determines the step size relative to the weight norm, up to the norm of the update direction. When update norms are fixed, this protects relative movement in each step from shrinking due to norm growth. But must norm control preserve relative movement at every step, or is it sufficient to preserve exploration capacity over the training trajectory as a whole? To examine this question, we begin with the measure of net displacement ∥ W T − W 0 ∥ F \lVert W_{T}-W_{0}\rVert_{F} . We develop a global perspective on norm control for Muon-type algorithms by examining exploration over entire training trajectories. This perspective identifies less restrictive norm-control conditions and guides the design of MuonGS , a new optimizer with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance. Central to our analysis is the accumulated effective learning rate , defined for general learning-rate schedules by C T = ∑ t = 0 T − 1 η t ∥ W t ∥ F . C_{T}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\frac{\eta_{t}}{\lVert W_{t}\rVert_{F}}. Our main claim is that continued exploration requires sufficient growth of C T C_{T} over the training intervals of interest. Further, we extend the displacement argument to arbitrary intervals and learning-rate schedules, that for bounded update directions, net weight displacement from iteration s s to T T , relative to the larger endpoint norm, is at most M ⁡ ( C T − C s ) M(C_{T}-C_{s}) . A large C T C_{T} may come mostly from early iterations. Continued exploration after iteration s s requires sufficient additional accumulation, C T − C s C_{T}-C_{s} , and if this increment is small, relative weight displacement over [ s , T ] [s,T] must also be small.

We next compare how different norm-control mechanisms affect this accumulation. When the learning rate η t = η \eta_{t}=\eta is held constant throughout training, vanilla Muon can exhibit linear norm growth and only logarithmic accumulation, C T = Θ ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) C_{T}=\Theta(\log T) . MuonW guarantees C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Omega(T) under the stated conditions, while fixed-norm control gives C T = Θ ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Theta(T) . These results show that weight decay and fixed-norm constraints guarantee at least linear accumulation, compared with vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst case. A direct consequence of our analysis is that bounded weight norms are sufficient for these linear accumulation guarantees, but stronger than needed to improve on vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst case. We show that this requirement can be relaxed to sufficiently slow norm growth, which still guarantees faster accumulation (as compared to vanilla Muon) even as weight norms increase and effective learning rates decrease. This observation opens up a broader family of Muon variants that control norm growth without requiring bounded weight norms. Can this additional flexibility be used to design optimizers that sustain accumulation throughout training and achieve better practical performance?

To investigate this question, we propose MuonGS , which uses Gram–Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of Muon’s update. The resulting update is orthogonal to the current weights in the Frobenius inner product. This orthogonality eliminates the first-order increase in the weight norm, so the norm grows only at second order in the step size. With bounded directions and a constant nominal learning rate, this guarantees O ⁡ ( t ) O(\sqrt{t}) norm growth and C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Omega(\sqrt{T}) , with the same accumulation order over later training windows. MuonGS thus improves vanilla Muon’s worst-case accumulation guarantee without fixing a radius. For smooth scale-invariant objectives, we further established the convergence rate for MuonGS. We evaluate MuonGS on FineWeb pretraining with modernized GPT-style models of approximately 160M and 400M parameters. At longer training horizons, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH. Fitting MuonH’s loss as a function of the training-token budget gives an estimated token-equivalent speedup of up to about 15 % 15\% at matched validation loss. In addition, MuonGS obtains lower validation perplexity than MuonH when pretraining a modern MoE model, having about 135M active and 1B total parameters, on Ultra-FineWeb. These results support MuonGS as a practical optimizer and demonstrate the value of relaxing norm-control requirements. Together with our theoretical guarantees, these findings provide a positive answer to the question above by showing that weaker norm control can indeed sustain accumulation throughout training while improving empirical performance. Our contributions are threefold. • We establish a global perspective on norm control in Muon, in the sense that we assess exploration over entire training trajectories through the growth of C T C_{T} and its increments over training intervals. Our analysis bounds relative weight displacement and, under scale-invariance and Lipschitz assumptions, attainable loss change. At a constant nominal learning rate, it distinguishes vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst case from the linear guarantees of MuonW and fixed-norm control. It also explains when norm growth can offset a larger nominal learning rate.

• We propose MuonGS and prove O ⁡ ( t ) O(\sqrt{t}) weight-norm growth, C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Omega(\sqrt{T}) , and C 2 ​ T − C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{2T}-C_{T}=\Omega(\sqrt{T}) for bounded directions and a constant nominal learning rate. These guarantees improvement on vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst-case accumulation without requiring bounded weight norms. The bound on C 2 ​ T − C T C_{2T}-C_{T} further shows that accumulation is sustained over later training windows, preserving a necessary condition for continued exploration. • We demonstrate MuonGS’s effectiveness in dense transformer pretraining at 160M and 400M parameter scale, with lower validation perplexity than MuonH at longer horizons and an estimated token-equivalent speedup of up to about 15 % 15\% at matched validation loss. In addition, we show MuonGS obtains lower validation perplexity than MuonH when pretraining a modern MoE model having about 135M active and 1B total parameters.

Weight Norm Control. Weight-norm control approaches have been commonly used in neural network training through reparameterization, shrinkage or constraints. Early works like weight normalization controlled weight geometry ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) . AdamW then decoupled weight decay from adaptive gradient preconditioning ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) , while AdamP and SGDP ( Heo et al., 2020 ) subsequently slowed norm growth by removing the radial component of the update for weights they detect as scale-invariant. Later methods introduced norm targets and per-matrix upper bounds ( Loshchilov, 2023 ; Franke et al., 2024 ) , followed by explicit constraints for LLM pretraining ( Loshchilov et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ; Hägele et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . However, these methods do not describe how fast the norm grows, nor do they analyze what impact the increased weight norm has on the overall algorithm performance.

Effective Learning Rate. The effective learning rate describes how parameter scale modifies the effect of a nominal learning rate. In scale-invariant settings, Van Laarhoven (2017) derived effective learning rates proportional to η / ‖ W ‖ 2 \eta/\|W\|^{2} for SGD and η / ‖ W ‖ \eta/\|W\| for RMSProp and Adam under their respective scaling assumptions. Later works related weight norms and decay to effective learning-rate schedules ( Hoffer et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ) , set up equivalences between weight decay and learning-rate schedules ( Li and Arora, 2019 ) , and studied related concepts such as spherical equilibrium, periodic behavior, and optimizer-dependent angular dynamics ( Wan et al., 2021 ; Lobacheva et al., 2021 ; Roburin et al., 2022 ; Kosson et al., 2023 ) . In LLM pretraining, the effective learning rate also helps explain why weight decay improves training ( D’Angelo et al., 2024 ) and why SGD underperforms Adam ( Glentis et al., 2026 ) . More recently, Liu et al. (2026) observed that effective learning rate determines the loss dynamics, while Amin et al. (2026) established stability results for effective learning-rate schedules. However, they do not explore how much the effective learning rate can accumulate over training, or relate this accumulation to exploration capacity.

chunks.section: 3 Norm Control Via Accumulated Effective Learning Rate
chunks.text: We begin with formalizing the global perspective on norm control by relating Muon’s exploration over training intervals to the accumulated effective learning rate C T C_{T} . Section 3.1 starts from what exploration means for a weight matrix of an LLM, derives the effective learning rate as the quantity that sets the size of a Muon step relative to the weights, and shows that the sum of effective learning rates over a training interval bounds how far training can explore in that interval. Section 3.2 compares how fast this sum grows under the three forms in which Muon is run in practice, without norm control, with decoupled weight decay, and with a fixed norm. Then it further answers whether a larger nominal learning rate can substitute for norm control. Proofs are collected in Appendix B .

To summarize, our analysis links norm control to exploration through accumulated effective learning rates. Weight decay and fixed-norm constraints sustain accumulation, while rapid norm growth can limit it and offset a larger nominal learning rate.

The preceding analysis links the benefit of bounded weight norms to the accumulation they preserve. This suggests relaxing the bounded-norm requirement, since sufficiently slow norm growth can still guarantee faster accumulation than vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst case. For example, at a constant nominal learning rate η > 0 \eta>0 , the bound r t ≤ r 0 + c ​ t a r_{t}\leq r_{0}+ct^{a} with c > 0 c>0 and 0 ≤ a < 1 0\leq a<1 gives C 2 ​ T − C T ≥ η ​ T r 0 + c ​ ( 2 ​ T ) a = Ω ⁡ ( T 1 − a ) . This opens up a broader family of Muon variants and brings us back to the question posed in the introduction. Can this additional flexibility be used to design optimizers that sustain accumulation throughout training and achieve better practical performance? We address this question with MuonGS , which controls norm growth by removing the radial component of Muon’s update. We analyze its accumulation and optimization properties, then evaluate its performance in LLM pretraining.

In this section we evaluate the MuonGS optimizer on the task of LLM pre-training. Since the results from Wen et al. (2026) indicate that the MuonH outperforms MuonW in typical pre-training settings, we focus our main comparison to MuonH. Note that both MuonGS and MuonH share the favorable property of not needing to tune a weight decay coefficient as opposed to MuonW. We include some additional results comparing with Muon and MuonW in Appendix A.1 . Below we present our main results using dense GPT-style models, but include preliminary results on MoE model training in Section 5.3 .

Architecture. We use the modernized GPT-style architecture from the Modded-NanoGPT Optimization Benchmark ( Jordan, 2026 ) at two scales, approximately 160M and 400M parameters. The smaller model, which corresponds to the NanoGPT model used in Jordan (2026) , has 12 layers, hidden width 768, and 6 attention heads; the other is a scaled-up version and has 24 layers, hidden width 1024, and 8 heads, with head dimension 128 for both sizes. Both models use RMSNorm, rotary positional embeddings, QK-Norm, squared-ReLU MLPs, and untied input and output embeddings. Pre-training setup. We pre-train on the 100B-token subset of the FineWeb dataset ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) using a sequence length of 1024 and a global batch of 512 sequences. Our experiments span approximately 3–25B training tokens for the 160M model and 8–63B for the 400M model, corresponding to roughly 1–8 Chinchilla budgets ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) at both scales. We use BF16 mixed-precision training. Optimizers. We compare MuonGS as described in Algorithm 1 with MuonH and Muon/MuonW. All methods use Nesterov momentum 0.95 0.95 for hidden matrix weights. AdamW is used for token embeddings, output-head weights, and all 1D parameters, with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.8 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.8,0.95) , ϵ = 10 − 10 \epsilon=10^{-10} , weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and respective max learning rates 0.7 0.7 , 0.004 0.004 , and 0.015 0.015 . Matrix and auxiliary learning rates decay linearly to zero without warmup after constant phases covering 15 % 15\% and 30 % 30\% of training, respectively.

Tuning and metrics. We tune learning rates on a multiplicative grid with ratio 2 \sqrt{2} similar to Wen et al. (2026) , separately for all optimizers, model sizes and training durations. For MuonW we additionally tune the weight decay as shown in Appendix A.1 . We use as metric the cross-entropy loss ℒ val \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}} over about 10M tokens from the FineWeb validation set, equivalently expressed as perplexity PPL = exp ⁡ ( ℒ val ) \mathrm{PPL}=\exp(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}) .

In this section we include preliminary results comparing MuonGS to MuonH on a modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. The model incorporates grouped-query attention ( Ainslie et al., 2023 ) , gated attention ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) and attention residuals (AttnRes) ( Team et al., 2026 ) . It has 32 layers, hidden width 512, and 64 routed experts with top-7 routing plus one shared expert per layer, yielding approximately 135M active non-embedding parameters and 1B total parameters. We train on Ultra-FineWeb ( Wang et al., 2025 ) for 10.8B and 21.6B tokens (i.e., 80 and 160 times the active parameters), using a batch size of 1,024 sequences of length 4,096. Learning rates are tuned on a 2 \sqrt{2} -spaced grid, with 2% warmup followed by linear decay to zero. Both MuonGS and MuonH use momentum 0.95 0.95 with Nesterov acceleration. From Figure 7 , we observe that MuonGS achieves lower best validation perplexity than MuonH at both training budgets, making it a promising method for modern MoE optimization.

We reexamined the role of weight norm control for Muon over the entire training trajectory instead of a single step. In particular, we use the accumulated effective learning rate to measure how far the weights can move relative to their norm over any training interval, and shows that continued exploration requires it to keep growing. We further show that vanilla Muon can only guarantee the accumulation to grow logarithmically, while weight norm control approaches such as weight decay and fixed-norm control guarantee a linear accumulation growth, which explains the role of weight norm control. Based on this finding, we relax the weight norm control to a larger range of approaches. In particular, we propose MuonGS by simply removing the radial component of the Muon update. Theoretically, we show that MuonGS guarantees an accumulation of at least T \sqrt{T} , sufficient for continued exploration. Numerically, MuonGS outperforms MuonW and MuonH at long training horizons, providing a speedup of up to 15 % 15\% at matched validation loss. Our accumulation guarantees are worst-case bounds, and the accumulation guarantee provides a necessary but not sufficient condition for continued exploration. Which rate of norm growth works best for a given training budget remains an open question.
